item.title: Qingdao leverages industrial design to drive manufacturing innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Qingdao leverages industrial design to drive manufacturing innovation Photo shows a refrigerator factory in COSMOPlat Industrial Internet Eco Park of Haier in Qingdao, east China's Shandong province. (Photo/Song Linji) In the summer of 2023, a user posted a message on the online platform of Haier, the Chinese home appliance giant headquartered in Qingdao, east China's Shandong province. The user expressed frustration over washing underwear and socks together in the same load, and casually attached a hand-drawn sketch with a question: "Could you develop a washing machine that washes these items separately?" Haier's designers quickly created prototype designs and shared them publicly. Over the next three months, more than 10,000 suggestions flooded in. Users took part throughout the development process, offering input on everything from compartment layouts to functional details. After the so-called "lazybones washing machine" was launched, it received 88,000 reservations within just seven days. The "lazybones" concept has since been extended to refrigerators, air conditioners, and other product categories, growing from a single product into an entire product line, and eventually into a broader family of products. To date, related products have sold more than 450,000 units in China. With designs adapted for different markets, they have also been exported to Italy, France, and other European countries. Textile products bound for overseas markets are manufactured in a workshop of a sock company in Qingdao, east China's Shandong province. (Photo/Liang Xiaopeng) This story illustrates the evolving role of industrial design in modern manufacturing. In Qingdao, industrial design is emerging as a "second core technology" that drives the transformation and upgrading of the manufacturing sector. "In the past, industrial design was often seen as 'dressing up' a product or giving it a particular look. Designers typically became involved only at the final stage of R&D, making established technologies and functions more appealing," said Pan Ping, director of the industrial policy division at the Qingdao municipal bureau of industry and information technology. "Today, industrial design starts with even the smallest pain points experienced by users, then works backward to define product functions, drive technological innovation, and reshape product design throughout the entire process," Pan told People's Daily. "In a nutshell, we have moved completely from 'we make what we have' to 'we create what users need,'" said Wu Jian, general manager of Haier's innovation design center, capturing the profound shift in the role of industrial design in recent years. Why has this change taken place? From a market perspective, industrial design itself is a means of differentiation. "In the past, production capacity was king, and products were highly homogeneous," Pan explained. "As consumer demand has evolved, people now place greater value on comfort, appearance, and emotional resonance. This is pushing companies beyond traditional production thinking and prompting them to use industrial design to unlock new product value and open up new market opportunities." At a deeper level, the shift reflects a natural requirement for China's manufacturing sector as it moves from "Made in China" toward greater original innovation. "For a long time, China's manufacturing industry was concentrated in the middle and lower reaches of global value chains. Industrial design helps address bottlenecks in the industry while transforming products from carriers of single functions into comprehensive experiences that integrate technology, aesthetics, culture and sustainability," Pan said. That is why industrial design is shedding its former role as a mere decorative afterthought and becoming a "second core technology" for improving manufacturing quality, efficiency and the ability to move up the value chain, Pan added. Engineers of Qingdao Hai Liya Group Co., Ltd. develop rescue ropes. (Photo courtesy of China Textile News) A change in mindset is only the first step. What matters is turning it into tangible results. At a laboratory of Qingdao Hai Liya Group Co., Ltd., a company specializing in industrial ropes, cables, ribbons, and emergency self-rescue safety equipment, an ordinary-looking rescue fanny pack was undergoing rigorous testing. Its rope resisted melting and charring at temperatures up to 204 degrees Celsius, while the descender boasted a breaking strength of 22 kilonewtons, well above national standards. In the event of a fire, the gear could be readied for deployment within seconds, 10 to 15 seconds faster than conventional fanny packs. "Traditional rescue fanny packs had limited functions, so firefighters needed to carry several sets of equipment for escape and rescue, making them heavy and cumbersome," an engineer from the company said. Starting from the actual needs of firefighters, the design team integrated descending, traversing, and lifting functions into a single fanny pack. The rope is 25 percent longer, while the overall weight has been reduced by 23 percent and the volume by 17 percent. The "integrated innovation" embodied in a fanny pack is a microcosm of how an entire city is mobilizing its resources to advance industrial design. Qingdao is an important hub for industrial design in north China. It has all 31 major manufacturing categories, four national advanced manufacturing clusters, two national manufacturing innovation centers, and six national demonstration bases for new industrialization. Its signature industrial chains such as smart home appliances and rail transit equipment, each boast an output value exceeding 100 billion yuan ($14.83 billion), offering abundant application scenarios for industrial design. Qingdao also adheres to the philosophy of "leading enterprises building platforms, and platforms driving industrial growth", establishing a full-coverage public service system featuring complementary and coordinated development. Spun off from Qingdao-based tire company Doublestar Group, Qingdao Lunyun Design and Research Institute Co., Ltd. focuses on the design and development of bio-based, green, and low-carbon tires, supporting over 20 upstream and downstream enterprises. Haier's innovation design center has established a national-level public service demonstration platform for small and medium-sized enterprises, with more than 90 percent of its design proposals making it into production. Home appliance manufacturer Hisense spun off its design division into Lixin, which provides design services to the group and to external clients. "Leading enterprises are stepping out of the internal loop of serving solely their own product lines. By opening up their proven design expertise and empowering small and medium-sized manufacturers either free of charge or at low cost, they are effectively driving Qingdao's manufacturing industry to accelerate its shift toward original design and homegrown independent brands," Pan said. In 2025, the revenue of industrial design enterprises above the designated size in Qingdao grew 22.1 percent year on year, while their total profits surged 102.2 percent. The operating profit margin of industrial enterprises above the designated size stood at 5.4 percent. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: How AI, energy empower each other across China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
How AI, energy empower each other across China BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- "Urgent orders tomorrow afternoon. Prioritize the production load and charge the batteries when power is cheap in the morning." This is the instruction a plant manager fed into an energy management system, with no coding or rule-setting required, and within seconds a complete scheduling strategy was generated. The system behind this technology is known as WHES OS, an artificial intelligence (AI)-native energy operating system developed by Weheng Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. It integrates an AI agent with "intent understanding," transforming energy storage from a rule-bound tool into an autonomous decision-maker that responds to natural language. This example offers a glimpse of a broader shift now underway across China's energy sector, where AI agents are rapidly being deployed in fields ranging from research and development (R&D) to operations and maintenance, safety monitoring and electricity market trading. Lyu Zhe, vice president of Beijing HyperStrong Technology Co., Ltd., a leading Chinese energy storage company, said AI is reshaping R&D by turning trial-and-error into predictive modeling and cutting development cycles from years to months, while on the operations side it boosts revenue by reducing unplanned outages and extending operating hours. In the case of safety monitoring, conventional threshold alarms often lag behind emerging problems, whereas AI uses deep learning to spot hidden risks before thermal runaway. The TENER Smart Storage platform developed by Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Ltd. can issue fault warnings up to seven days in advance and pinpoint fault causes within five minutes. In electricity trading, AI optimizes charging and discharging strategies by forecasting prices based on variables including renewable energy output, weather, grid congestion and market quotes. Notably, at Envision Group's smart storage station in Binzhou, east China's Shandong Province, an AI trading agent has achieved 95 percent accuracy in predicting peak-valley price spreads. These applications point to a wider intelligent shift taking shape in China's energy landscape, underpinned by a policy push for greater coordination between computing and electricity. This endeavor has gained momentum in 2026, with multiple official signals released this year. This year's government work report called for launching new infrastructure projects on hyper-scale intelligent computing clusters and coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply -- the first time such a provision has appeared in the document. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan, meanwhile, calls for promoting the coordinated deployment of green electricity and computing power. A plan for developing a new energy system during the 15th Five-Year Plan period further calls for ensuring high-quality electricity supply for sectors including big data and AI. AI is a strategic technology driving a new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, but the computing centers behind it guzzle electricity in staggering amounts, with volatile loads and sudden demand spikes. In 2025, China's data centers consumed 170 billion kWh of electricity, or 1.6 percent of the nation's total power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). A China Galaxy Securities report projects that this figure will exceed 700 billion kWh by 2030, breaching the 5-percent mark. Such soaring demand is matched by a robust supply side. China is home to the world's largest and fastest-growing renewable energy system. The NEA announced on Tuesday that installed photovoltaic capacity had surpassed coal-fired power capacity for the first time, making solar the country's largest power source by installed capacity. "Only by combining the innovative strengths of China's domestically developed large AI models with the country's robust power supply capacity, particularly its abundant clean energy, can China turn its advantages in energy and electricity into competitive strengths in the AI industry," said Ding Zhaohao, a professor at North China Electric Power University. In May, four Chinese authorities unveiled an action plan, envisioning that by 2030, the clean energy supply capacity for AI computing power infrastructure will be significantly increased, while the application of AI in the energy sector will also be considerably improved. The plan calls for coordinating the development of large renewable energy bases with national computing hubs, directing more computing facilities to energy-rich regions where they can tap into abundant local renewable power. In Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, a pilot project is paving the way. The country's first data center project that integrates renewable generation, storage and computing load went into operation in July 2025. It runs on self-generated wind and solar power, with the surplus stored in batteries and the grid reserved as a backup option. The early results are encouraging, yet the road to deeper integration is not without challenges, including a shortage of industry-specific large AI models, a limited supply of high-quality industry data, and inadequate mechanisms for cross-enterprise and cross-industry data sharing. Yuan Jun, vice president of the National Data Development Research Institute, said coordinated efforts should be made in policy mechanisms, development planning, market systems and technical standards. item.title: China's service trade posts steady expansion, as travel, transport lead export growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
China's service trade posts steady expansion, as travel, transport lead export growth BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's trade in services maintained steady growth in the first seven months of 2026, as the export of travel and transport services drove more than half of the overall export expansion, official data showed Thursday. The country's services trade totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan (about 655.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the period, up 8.3 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. During the period, services exports rose 17.1 percent year on year to over 1.77 trillion yuan. Services imports reached 2.67 trillion yuan, up 3.2 percent from a year earlier. The country's services trade deficit narrowed by 176.33 billion yuan from a year earlier to 900.25 billion yuan. A breakdown of the data showed travel and transport services emerged as the two export growth drivers. Travel services exports surged 27.7 percent, while transport services exports rose 27.1 percent. The two categories contributed 22.1 percent and 29.9 percent, respectively, to the overall growth of services exports. Knowledge-intensive services also remained a pillar of China's export mix. Trade in such services, which include telecommunications, information technology, finance, intellectual property and other business services, increased 6.6 percent to 1.96 trillion yuan, accounting for 44.1 percent of the country's total services trade. China has intensified policy efforts to boost service sector development. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and this year's government work report both made specific arrangements for this sector. In April, the State Council issued a guideline on advancing the expansion and quality upgrading of the sector. According to the guideline, China aims to make marked progress in high-quality service sector development by 2030, with the total scale of the sector exceeding 100 trillion yuan by then, while more competitive and influential "China services" brands will be cultivated. item.title: China unveils five-year plan to promote SME development
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
China unveils five-year plan to promote SME development BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has issued a plan to promote high-quality development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) during the 2026-2030 period, setting targets for business growth, innovation and the development environment. By 2030, China's SMEs are expected to achieve growth in both quality and scale, with per capita operating revenue of major SMEs posting cumulative growth of around 15 percent over the five-year period, according to the plan, which was jointly issued by 10 government departments, including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The plan describes SMEs as an important force in driving innovation, creating jobs and improving people's livelihoods. It calls for efforts to improve systems for cultivating high-quality enterprises and providing public services, strengthen the legal and policy framework, and ensure better access to factors of production and a more supportive development environment. SMEs contribute roughly 70 percent of China's technological innovation, 60 percent of its gross domestic product, and 80 percent of its urban employment, according to an OECD report on SME financing. SMEs' innovation capacity will be notably enhanced, with average annual growth in internal research and development expenditure by major industrial SMEs targeted at over 8 percent and the number of "little giant" firms expected to reach 22,000 by 2030, according to the plan. "Little giant" firms refer to the novel elites of SMEs that are engaged in manufacturing, specialize in a niche market and boast cutting-edge technologies. The plan calls for continued improvements to the SME service system and an increase in the number of cooperation zones for Chinese and foreign SMEs to 50 by 2030. By then, the development environment for SMEs is expected to improve further, with a sound long-term mechanism for resolving payment arrears owed to SMEs largely in place and access to diversified financing further broadened. The plan sets out seven key tasks, including keeping businesses and employment stable, strengthening enterprise cultivation, accelerating digital, intelligent and green development, promoting coordinated and integrated development, improving the supply of production factors, strengthening the SME service system, and enhancing legal and policy safeguards. It further specifies measures that include helping SMEs develop trademark and brand strategies, and launching the second phase of a national SME development fund, among others. "SMEs face strategic opportunities, as well as risks and challenges, as a new round of sci-tech revolution and industrial transformation gathers pace and competition among major countries grows more complex and intense," said an MIIT official. The official said that, in response to new circumstances, China needs to step up policy support, strengthen reform and innovation measures, boost SMEs' internal drivers of growth, and reinforce the foundations of the real economy. The plan is expected to open up more pathways for SME transformation and upgrading, said Ma Yuan, deputy director of the Institute for Enterprise Research under the Development Research Center of the State Council. Supporting SME development is among the priorities of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), which calls for promoting the growth of SMEs that use specialized and sophisticated technologies to produce novel and unique products, reducing computing costs for SMEs, and strengthening services to support their digital and intelligent transformation. This year's government work report also pledged stronger support for SMEs undergoing digital and intelligent transformation. China made notable progress in SME development during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), with more than 63 million SMEs operating nationwide by the end of 2025, accounting for over 95 percent of all business entities. item.title: China commemorates 81st anniversary of victory against Japanese aggression
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
China commemorates 81st anniversary of victory against Japanese aggression Student pay floral tributes to martyrs at a memorial hall for the western Yunnan campaign during the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, in Tengchong, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Gong Zujin/Xinhua) BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- People across China held commemorative activities on Thursday to mark the 81st anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) was the first to break out and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded. Japan officially surrendered on Sept. 2, 1945, by signing the Instrument of Surrender. The war marked China's first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times. Through immense sacrifice, the Chinese people made a major contribution to the salvation of human civilization and the defense of world peace. In 2014, China's national legislature designated Sept. 3 as Victory Day of its War of Resistance. Last year, China held grand commemorative events in Beijing on Sept. 3 to mark the 80th anniversary of the victory, including a military parade in Tian'anmen Square. On Thursday, a symposium was held in Beijing to commemorate the 81st anniversary. Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event. About 200 people took part in the symposium, including veterans of the war, relatives of wartime commanders and fallen soldiers, and international friends who contributed to China's victory, as well as representatives of their families. Officials, young military personnel, and student representatives spoke at the event, vowing to remember history, honor fallen heroes, cherish peace, and build a better future. In Harbin, capital of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, a series of activities commemorating the hard-won victory 81 years ago was held at the Northeast China Revolutionary Martyrs' Memorial Hall. Representatives from government agencies, businesses, military units, schools and social organizations attended a memorial event and paid silent tribute to those who fell in the War of Resistance. They also visited an exhibition featuring wartime relics to learn more about the historical significance and contemporary relevance of the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (NAJUA). For 14 years, the soldiers of NAJUA fought in extreme conditions, suffering severe food and clothing shortages while facing overwhelming enemy superiority. Yet they still inflicted heavy losses on Japanese forces, making an indelible contribution to the World Anti-Fascist War. "We commemorate the victory so that we do not forget history," said Tong Guobo, head of the memorial hall. "The NAJUA spirit -- of unwavering faith, deep patriotism, and dauntless courage -- has taken deep root in northeast China, inspiring generations to forge ahead." At the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders in east China's Jiangsu Province, people took part in poetry readings and historical reenactments, bringing to life the harrowing stories of that dark chapter for the audience. College students recite poems during a ceremony marking the 81st anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War at the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Bo) "Both my parents were survivors of the Nanjing Massacre, and we lost six family members to the Japanese forces in 1937," said Cao Yuli, who was participating in the event. "We should always remember the past and value the peace we enjoy today," said Zhang Xinjue, a student choir member during the commemorations. In east China's Shandong Province, more than 3,000 artifacts that bear witness to the Japanese atrocities are exhibited at a private museum in Pingyin County. Among them are military postcards and letters and soldiers' diaries, as well as photographs, combat maps, and other items such as swords, helmets, and gas masks. Han Guangyou, the 65-year-old curator of the museum, has spent more than four decades amassing these artifacts from across China. "These exhibits stand as undeniable proof of the war crimes committed by imperial Japan," he said. The museum now receives more than 20,000 visitors annually. Han is currently collaborating with several universities to catalog, digitize and research the collection. "These stark exhibits serve as a sobering reminder for young people to remember the lessons of history and strive to build a stronger China," Han said. "Today's world is far from peaceful," said Zhang Shaoduo, an associate researcher at Shanghai International Studies University. "These commemorative events remind people across the globe that a stronger China remains a pillar of world peace." Also on Thursday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urged Japanese right-wing forces to adhere to the path of peaceful development, in response to Japan's record-high defense budget request for the 2027 fiscal year. "Our solemn message to Japanese right-wing forces: the right way forward for Japan is to fulfill its international obligations, fully remove the pernicious influence of militarism, and keep to peaceful development," Guo told a regular press briefing in Beijing. item.title: Across rivers and ridges -- China ensures school access for children
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Across rivers and ridges -- China ensures school access for children KUNMING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- At age 12, Lei Xin had already mastered a skill most adults would never attempt: navigating a treacherous cliffside trail in the dark -- not for adventure, but to go to school. For years, reaching school meant a three-hour trek for Lei and his peers from Nizhuhe Village in Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. The village sits at the bottom of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon near the border with Guizhou Province, while their school is perched more than 500 meters above them on the cliffs. Children used to leave home well before sunrise, often returning exhausted. For parents, the daily trek was a source of constant worry. Now, the most daunting stretch of the route Lei once took to school can be covered in just 57 seconds, with a new 288-meter-high cliffside elevator whisking students up the canyon wall at five meters per second. An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 29, 2026 shows cliffside elevators at the Nizhu River Grand Canyon in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. (Xinhua/Chen Xinbo) Lei's story is not unique. Across China's vast, often rugged frontier regions, millions of children face long, perilous journeys to school. From sheer cliffs to winding rivers, the obstacles vary, but so do the solutions. The efforts, backed by national policy, reflect a broader commitment -- ensuring that geography does not determine a child's access to education. CROSSING EVERY DIVIDE Guanzhai Primary School, perched on the cliffs above, serves children from surrounding mountain communities, including four in Nizhuhe Village. Cut off from the school above by sheer cliffs, the children had to follow a rudimentary trail carved into a rock face hundreds of meters high. Narrow and steep, strewn with loose gravel, the trail had sections barely half a meter wide. The steepest stretches required them to climb by hand. "Back then, I wasn't afraid my child would be tired. I was afraid something might happen to him on the way," said Zhao Suzhen, the mother of Lei, who had accompanied him along the treacherous trail countless times over the years. LEFT: An undated file photo shows students from Nizhuhe Village climbing a cliff on their way to school in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province; RIGHT: This photo taken by Xinhua photographer Chen Xinbo on Aug. 29, 2026 shows cliffside elevators in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. (Xinhua) The change came with the development of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon scenic area. In 2022, a 268-meter-high elevator and an aerial cable car system came into service, giving children from the deep mountains a "sky shuttle" to the clifftop school. A second elevator, rising 288 meters, opened at the end of July this year as visitor numbers grew. Together, the two elevators can carry up to 1,200 passengers per hour, significantly boosting the scenic area's capacity while eliminating the congestion that once forced students to compete with tourists for rides during peak seasons. Now, the entire journey from the village to school takes about 30 minutes. Students take a shuttle bus to the foot of the cliff, ride an elevator, then continue by cable car to reach the school. Students take cable cars on their way to school in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Xinbo) On Aug. 30, as many primary and secondary schools across Yunnan welcomed students back for the new semester, Lei once again boarded his unusual ride. Stepping into the new elevator, he watched the numbers on the display tick upward. "The first elevator takes 90 seconds. This one, 33 seconds faster," he said, sharing his calculation. "I feel like an immortal carrying me through the sky." Free for local students and villagers, the "sky shuttle" also features dedicated student passages, with police officers and staff on hand during peak hours to keep the children safe. By the end of August, the service had safely carried nearly 1,000 student trips between the village and school. More than 500 km away from Puli Township, which administers Nizhuhe Village, another group of children in Yunnan began the school day on the water. Students are pictured aboard a ferry in Bo'ai Town of Funing County, Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Guansen) At a ferry crossing in Banda Village of Bo'ai Town, located in a reservoir area, village official Liang Guoyou arrived early in the morning to help students board. One by one, the children stepped onto a ferry that carried them across the water. It's their version of a "school bus." The journey was not always this secure. "Years ago, privately operated ferries lacked unified standards, and safety was a constant concern," Liang said. Since 2021, local authorities have worked with schools, parents and transport officials to build a coordinated school transport system. Seven dedicated ferries now serve 12 crossings across the township for 329 primary and secondary school students and preschoolers. For 55-year-old ferryman Wei Jinlin, the difference could not be starker. "When I was young, getting to school meant walking nearly 20 kilometers to town," he said. "Now the children can take the ferry. It's much safer and far more convenient." According to local authorities, the ferry routes have safely carried students more than 147,000 times over the years, covering over 70,000 kilometers in total. A transportation law enforcer inspects a ferry in Funing County, Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Aug. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Guansen) Across China, governments are tailoring school transport to local needs, finding different ways to close the distance between home and school. In March, mountainous Chengkou County of southwest China's Chongqing Municipality launched a "Hope Line" school bus service, with 33 dedicated routes now in operation. The service uses fixed routes combined with flexible pickup points to tackle the "last mile" challenge for students living in scattered rural communities. In Panxi Town, Guizhou, authorities faced similar challenges reaching students scattered across remote areas and recently surveyed the travel needs of 121 students before launching three customized school bus routes. Four vehicles now connect eight villages, providing point-to-point service during school hours. BEYOND SCHOOL RIDES The impact, it turns out, goes far beyond the ride to school. Li Zhiguang, principal of Guanzhai Primary School, said that as the "sky shuttle" has made the journey less daunting and physically demanding, students become more cheerful, confident and engaged in school life. "They are more willing to speak up in class and eager to explore the wider world," Li added. They also have more time for the things they enjoy. "Now I can use those hours saved on the journey to read and exercise," said Wang Sichun, a third-grade student at the school, her voice bright. An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 30, 2026 shows the Guanzhai Primary School at the top of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. (Xinhua/Chen Xinbo) The benefits ripple outward. The "sky shuttle" has also enabled local co-development of education and rural revitalization. As the canyon's scenery and cliff elevators attracted more visitors, Zhao turned part of her home into a three-story guesthouse with 12 rooms. During peak season, bookings can be made weeks in advance. "Now I can look after my children while earning a living without leaving my hometown," she said. More villagers are following suit, opening guesthouses, selling local specialties or working as guides. Official data show that Puli Township now boasts 46 guesthouses and 159 specialty restaurants, with tourism supporting nearly 3,500 jobs. Cai Xiong, chairman of the company behind the elevator project, grew up in the mountains himself and watched generations of children make the arduous climb to school. "I know how difficult the journey can be," he said. "I hope the 'sky shuttle' can give them a safer way to school, so they can focus on their studies, pursue their dreams and one day give back to their hometown." Yang Bin, a professor at Yunnan Normal University who has long studied education development in western China, praised the local approach of repurposing cultural tourism infrastructure for public educational services. "This is not merely an improvement in transportation infrastructure. It is a safeguard of rural children's right to education, ensuring that frontier children truly have access to equitable and quality schooling," Yang said. He added that better educational conditions also support rural revitalization by helping to retain population and stabilize communities, providing a lasting social foundation for tourism and other industries. Students greet a staff member before taking the cliffside elevator at Nizhu River Grand Canyon in Puli Township, Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Xinbo) The efforts are now finding institutional backing. A national plan to build a strong country through education by 2035 calls for advancing high-quality, balanced compulsory education and greater integration of urban and rural education, while narrowing gaps among regions, schools and student groups. Earlier this year, China issued a plan to accelerate agricultural and rural modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), calling for stronger basic public services in rural areas. It specifically requires more balanced compulsory education and better conditions for rural schools, including necessary small-scale village schools and kindergartens. Yang noted that these efforts can help address the longstanding challenges in rural education and narrow the urban-rural development gap. "The road to school is, in many ways, the first step toward educational equity," he said. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Traditional autumn harvest display attracts tourists to village in E China's Jiangxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Traditional autumn harvest display attracts tourists to village in E China's Jiangxi Villagers dry harvested crops in Huangling village, Wuyuan county, Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province. (People's Daily Online/Kong Wenjin) Recently, in Huangling village, Wuyuan county, Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province, local villagers placed red peppers, corn, pumpkins, beans and other crops in bamboo trays and set them on wooden racks attached to Hui-style houses to dry. The colorful trays set against the ancient buildings, with their white walls and dark-tiled roofs, create a striking scene that draws many tourists. Built on the mountainside, Huangling has little flat land, so rooftops have become the main place for drying crops, a local tradition known as shaiqiu, or autumn crop sun-drying. This tradition has evolved into a distinctive folk custom celebrating a good harvest, allowing visitors to experience the charm of traditional farming culture and the joy of the harvest amid a vibrant autumn scene. Villagers dry harvested crops in Huangling village, Wuyuan county, Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida) GYIRONG, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Power supply has been restored to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, the State Grid said on Thursday. Despite risks such as landslides and frequent rockfalls, frontline personnel worked around the clock to restore temporary power lines in the core area of the port at 8 p.m. Thursday, the company said.
